query: Earlier studies reported high hardness and compressive strength in AlCrCuFeNiTi, CuFeNiMnTi, and low-density AlCrFeTiX high-entropy alloys. However, some AlCrFeTiX alloys were brittle at 25 °C, and AlCrFeTiCo showed only 1.8% plastic strain at 600 °C. Because these findings concern different alloy systems, they do not explain the deformation behavior or the relatively low hardness and strength of equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in its simple solid-solution state, despite its favorable plasticity and machinability. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs this combination of deformation, hardness, and strength and why? Define a controlled comparison that would distinguish the proposed explanation, predict observations relative to the starting alloy, state the composition, state, temperature, and loading limits of the hypothesis, identify the prior evidence supporting its premise, and specify results that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The relatively low hardness and strength but high plasticity of equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in the as-quenched single–phase state are governed primarily by the absence of nanoscale ordered Ti-rich B2 (NiTi/CoTi–type) precipitates; introducing such precipitates by controlled aging will raise the critical resolved shear stress and hardness while concurrently reducing uniform plastic strain. Thus, precipitation (or its absence) is the single microstructural lever that dictates the observed deformation–strength–ductility balance.
generation.material_initial_state: Vacuum-induction–melted, homogenised (1150 °C, 24 h) and water-quenched equimolar CoCrFeNiTi alloy forming a single-phase FCC solid solution (no detectable second phases by XRD/TEM).
generation.intervention: Isothermal aging at 700 ± 10 °C for 24 h in Ar to promote coherent Ti-rich B2 precipitation (followed by water quench).
generation.conditions: Mechanical tests at 25 °C and 600 °C in compression (strain rate 10⁻³ s⁻¹) up to 30 % true strain or fracture, in laboratory air.
generation.structural_mediator: Volume fraction, size (~5–50 nm), and number density of coherent B2 (NiTi/CoTi-type) precipitates within the FCC matrix.
generation.mechanism: Ordered B2 precipitates provide Orowan and order-hardening barriers to dislocation glide, raising CRSS and Vickers hardness. Their elastic modulus and interfacial mismatch elevate local stresses, facilitating crack initiation and reducing work-hardening capacity, thereby decreasing uniform plastic strain and machinability. In the quenched alloy, the lack of such obstacles enables easy dislocation slip, giving low hardness/strength and good ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: After aging: (a) Vickers hardness will increase by ≥150 % (e.g., 200 HV → ≥500 HV); (b) 0.2 % yield strength in compression will rise by ≥2× at 25 °C and ≥1.5× at 600 °C; (c) plastic strain to fracture at 25 °C will fall from >15 % to <5 %; (d) TEM will reveal 5–50 nm B2 precipitates with number densities >10²² m⁻³ absent in the baseline.
generation.baseline: Same alloy in the water-quenched, single-phase FCC condition tested under identical loading and temperature conditions.
generation.boundary: Hypothesis applies to equimolar (±2 at. %) CoCrFeNiTi aged 600–800 °C where diffusion allows B2 nucleation but avoids extensive coarsening. Alloys containing ≥5 at.% Al, Nb, or Mo, or those processed by severe plastic deformation, are outside the defined scope.
generation.uncertainty: Exact precipitate number density and consequent quantitative strength increment depend on unknown nucleation kinetics; predicted magnitude (≥150 % hardness increase, ≥2× yield strength) could vary by ±30 %.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of CoCrFeNiTi coupons: (i) water-quenched (single-phase), (ii) water-quenched + 700 °C/24 h aging. Confirm phases by XRD and HRTEM/EDS mapping. Measure Vickers hardness (500 g, 15 s) at ≥10 indents/sample and compressive stress–strain curves at 25 °C and 600 °C (strain rate 10⁻³ s⁻¹).
measurements: Plastic strain to fracture (%) at 25 °C and 600 °C
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if aged samples either (1) show no detectable B2 nanoscale precipitates, or (2) exhibit <30 % increase in hardness AND <30 % increase in yield strength compared with baseline, or (3) retain plastic strain to fracture >10 % at 25 °C despite confirmed B2 precipitation.
